blocks.x: While movies like Akira and Ghost in the Shell were what piqued my initial interest in Japanese anime, leading to a lifelong obsession with Japanese culture, there were other anime series that had a major impact on me, further deepening my already strong interest in Japanese anime. One of the most important of those was Cowboy Bebop, the classic anime from 1998.

I decided to do a rewatch of this series, not just for my own purposes (I had forgotten much), but also to introduce my son to this anime masterpiece. While watching, in the back of my mind was the thought: What makes this series so great? This article is to my attempt to answer that question.

As for what made a hit, surely some of it was luck to be in the right place at the right time, in an era when Japanese anime was beginning to get popular, and newly minted anime fans were growing. But I can clearly say it wasn’t a fad, there is a lot of real greatness to Cowboy Bebop. Like many successful works, it isn’t one thing but a synergistic combination of a handful that make it great. Let’s address those one at a time.
Genre Blend

Cowboy Bebop is a unique blend of three genres: Science fiction, western, and film noir. I’m a huge fan of SciFi, not so much of western, and to be honest I was only vaguely familiar with what film noir is. I did a bit of research and, while the elements of noir are straightforward, most of its famous movies are quite old (60s, etc.) and I haven’t seen any of the classics. Of the more modern ones, one of the few I’ve seen and enjoyed was Mulholland Drive.

I haven’t gone back and did any detailed analysis, but I feel like many of the scenes in Cowboy Bebop focus on one of these three genres, and yet as a whole things are stitched together very well. The genres provide pools of context and ideas to draw from, but the production and story makes things coherent and enjoyable.
The genre blend also influences the settings, which are a mix of scifi-ish cityscapes, noir-like rundown buildings, and western-like expansive areas.
Characters

There are only a handful of main characters, but not only are they unique and well-defined, but they all interact in natural ways with the others. I feel like each of the characters is very consistent, and there was no point when I was jumping out of my seat to surprise or frustration with an out-of-character action. Rather, often I get the feeling like “Yeah, I knew he would do that!” which to me keeps me interested and involved. There’s a good mix of male and female characters, with diversity in the ages in the main characters.

Cute animals also make up an important minority, with one semi-major character (a dog) and a few others scattered throughout. Minor characters are pretty diverse with different races and other characteristics.

While a huge amount of time isn’t devoted to it overall, there are a few key scenes and story beats that advance the character’s background or history in some important way, and that makes the characters more believable.
Self-contained Formulaic Story

Except for a few at the beginning and end, most of the 26 episodes are independent stories, and each has only a little over 20 minutes to tell their tale. I don’t love all episodes equally, but I can appreciate how the storytelling is very consistent, and very smart about how it introduces a problem and then has a few twists before resolving it in a satisfying, comedic, and/or dramatic way.
The storytelling is similar to the consistency of the characters. You know what to expect in terms of a well-crafted story, and you get it time after time.
Often there is a gun battle in the second half of the episode, and these too are extremely efficient, cutting to the point instead of having drawn-out extended battle scenes.
Cinematography

One thing I realized on my rewatch of Cowboy Bebop is that the cinematography is really good, to the point that it looks like it was crafted with the same love and thought done for a high-quality (classic) hollywood film. In fact, one of the credits was for 撮影監督 (satsuei kantoku), a role that literally translates to “cinematograper”.

Surely some of this is due to limitations at animation at the time, but each “shot” feels well thought out, and leverages techniques like dutch angles, wide-angle lenses, juxtaposition, time adjustments, lighting, etc. There is one key scene that I don’t want to spoil in case you haven’t seen it yet, but it involves slowed down time and a flock of doves and is utterly beautiful.
I am sure there are many other anime since then take this sort of care, but I can’t think of any that came before it. If you know any, let me know in the comments!
Music

Cowboy Bebop is the first anime I watched with soundtrack by Yoko Kanno, and she has grown to become my favorite composer and performer for anime music. After listening to many of her tracks you start to notice patterns (like a chorus at key parts), but overall she is extremely creative and great, emulating a wide gamut of styles.
Having said that, I don’t love all of the songs in Cowboy Bebop. At times they seem random don’t really fit the scene, but overall I appreciate the diversity.

Several of the songs with English singing sound somehow unnatural in their lyrics and/or singing style, but even so those are the ones that stick with me. The exception is the (every episode) ending song that I really just don’t enjoy.
While I’ve never done it myself (at least for Cowboy Bebop) I used to know people who listened to this series’s entire soundtrack over and over. Indeed there is really some good music here.

I talked about three genres being blended for this series, but I think it’s fair to say that at least musically, Jazz (and obviously the subgenre Bebop) is a 4th genre that creates a wonderful atmosphere, enhancing the darker and more complex aspects of the production.
Story

Ironically, I don’t think the overarching story itself is that great, considering the parts at the end and beginning of the series that are connected. It feels like there isn’t a lot of detail about what is happening, though there is enough to keep things interesting. It seems this sort of vague story is a characteristic of film noir, so in that sense it’s consistent with that genre.
But honestly story has never been my number one priority, with things like characters, atmosphere, and visual/audio production being higher.
Japanese

I always try to add a bit of info on the difficulty of the Japanese for those studying the language. Overall, this series uses a lot of domain-specific words (like 賞金首 [shoukin-kubi] that means a bounty being hunted, not something that typically comes up) and a good amount of slang and expressions, such that even on a second watch I had trouble with a few parts. But the diverse and out-of-ordinary Japanese only contributes to the uniqueness of the series.
Even if you aren’t likely to use many of these words in your daily life (unless you happen to be appearing in a SciFi or Noir film), they are fun to learn and understand.

By the way, lately I have been developing a website that allows you to extract and study the vocab words from anime episodes, so I decided to exact the words from the first episode of Cowboy Bebop in case you want to check it out here.
Concluding Thoughts

I hesitate to oversimplify, but I feel like Cowboy Bebop takes a few ideas and tries to do them cleanly, consistently, and artistically, without trying to bite off more than it can chew. It uses little surprises, like a plot twist here or there, as opposed to sudden changes in character, theme, or concept. And it is this very consistency (plus realistic writing and well-executed visuals and music) that really draws you into the story and keeps you interested. Longer series like Naruto and One Piece were fun the first few tens of episodes, but after major changes I just tend to get bored.

I made a surprising discovery about an apparent connection between one of Cowboy Bebop’s main characters and Ki Aikido, which I already wrote about here. And if you are interested in the Netflix remaking of Cowboy Bebop, I’ll just say I highly recommend against watching it.

If you haven’t seen the Cowboy Bebop anime and are a fan or Japanese culture or anime, it’s definitely a must-see. If you aren’t into anime but still enjoy any of the above-mentioned genres, I think you’ll probably enjoy it. Even if you aren’t in either group, there’s a good chance you’ll enjoy a good part of it.

On a final note, I was struggling to decide which I like better: Cowboy Bebop or Samurai Champloo, anime series by the same director (Shinichiro Watanabe). It’s a really tough call, and they share a lot of things in common in terms of the characters and story design, but I think I like Samurai Champloo a little more. Carol & Tuesday is another pretty good series from the same director.
Now if I can only get a certain song out of my head…
